clauses.clause: Share accurate information about a topic (C)
clauses.note: Students share observations drawn from videos and text about what happens during day and night; the information is grounded in what they observed, making it accurate.

clauses.clause: Use a variety of communication modes to share information (C)
clauses.note: Students share information orally via partner talk (Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face, turn and talk) and whole-group share-outs, and they sort picture cards into categories (a visual/physical mode). However, the modes are predominantly oral; the variety is thin — students do not write, draw, or present through a distinctly different communication mode beyond speaking and sorting, so the 'variety of different modes' clause is only partially met.

verdicts.evidence: 'I noticed that during the day, people and animals __________.'
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to share relevant and accurate information through a variety of different modes (C — construction). Students share relevant, accurate observations about daytime and nighttime activities drawn from the text and videos. In the Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face protocol, students use the sentence frame "I noticed that during the day, people and animals __________" to share information with a partner, and selected students share out to the whole group. Students also sort picture cards into daytime/nighttime categories and explain their sorting. However, the "variety of different modes" clause is only partially met: the communication modes are predominantly oral (partner talk, whole-group share-out), with sorting as a secondary physical/visual mode; students do not share information through writing, drawing, or a distinctly different presentation mode, making the variety thin.

clauses.note: Students respond to a question about why the author chose a particular technique, touching on author purpose/craft, but the activity does not explicitly have students discern the overall purpose of the text (e.g., to inform, to entertain, to persuade). The student response addresses a narrow authorial choice rather than the text's purpose.

clauses.clause: Evaluate the extent to which texts achieve their purposes based on author, audience, and context

verdicts.evidence: 'Why do you think the author describes the sun and moon in this way?' (to show imagination)
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to (1) develop and apply knowledge of author, audience, and context to discern/establish the purpose of texts, and (2) evaluate the extent to which texts achieve those purposes. Students engage with a narrow aspect of authorial purpose when they answer "'Why do you think the author describes the sun and moon in this way?' (to show imagination)" and "'What do you think the author means when she writes 'what the sun sees' and 'what the moon sees?'" — these touch on author's choices and context but do not explicitly ask students to identify the overall purpose of the text or to evaluate how well the text achieves that purpose. The evaluate clause is entirely absent: no activity asks students to judge whether the text successfully meets its purpose. Because one clause is thinly/partially addressed and the other is not met, alignment is partial.

clauses.clause: Work with others to solve problems
Work with others to explore and create texts

verdicts.evidence: Tell students that as they watch the videos, they should look carefully to see what they notice and observe about the sky, the sun, the moon, and what animals and people are doing during the daytime and during the nighttime. Tell students they should also think about the questions they have as they watch the videos.
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to work with others to (a) discuss topics, (b) investigate questions, (c) solve problems, and (d) explore and create texts. Clauses (a) and (b) are met: students collaboratively discuss the topic of day and night through multiple turn-and-talk and Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face partner protocols (e.g., "Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner: 'What did the sun "see" animals and people doing during the daytime?'"), and they investigate questions about daytime/nighttime by sorting picture cards in pairs and sharing observations after watching videos. However, there is no activity in which students work together to solve a problem (clause c), and no activity in which students collaboratively explore or create a text (clause d) — the texts are teacher-read-alouds and the sorting activity produces categorized picture cards, not a text.

In Work Time A, they listen to What the Sun Sees, What the Moon Sees and answer questions like 'What did the sun "see" animals and people doing during the daytime?' The OR-list rule applies: satisfying any one of the four purposes (build knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, share information/ideas) is sufficient, and students clearly use the texts to build knowledge about day/night activities.
